text: Edmund Burke (/bɜːrk/; 12 January [NS] 1729[2] – 9 July 1797) was an Anglo-Irish writer, philosopher, and politician widely credited as the founder of the cultural and political philosophy of conservatism.[3] Regarded as one of the most influential conservative thinkers and political writers of the 18th century,[4] Burke served as a member of Parliament (MP) from 1766 to 1794 in the House of Commons of Great Britain with the Whig Party. His writings significantly influenced public opinion in both Great Britain and France following the French Revolution in 1789,[5] and he remains a major figure in modern conservative circles. Burke advocated for underpinning societal virtues with manners and emphasized the importance of religious institutions for moral stability and the good of the state,[6] themes expressed in his satirical work, A Vindication of Natural Society (1756). He criticized the British government's actions toward the American colonies, particularly its taxation policies, supporting the colonists' right to resist metropolitan authority while opposing their pursuit of independence. He is also remembered for his long-term support of Catholic emancipation, the impeachment of Warren Hastings from the East India Company, and his opposition to the French Revolution. In 1774, Burke was elected MP for Bristol. In his Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), he argued that the revolution was destroying traditional institutions and good society and condemned the persecution of the Catholic Church that followed. This led to his becoming a leading figure in the conservative faction of the Whig Party, which he called the Old Whigs, in contrast to the pro-French Revolution New Whigs led by Charles James Fox.[7] Burke maintained close relationships with public intellectuals such as Samuel Johnson, David Garrick, Oliver Goldsmith, and Joshua Reynolds. In his debates, he consistently opposed unrestricted ruling power and championed political parties' ability to maintain principled opposition to prevent abuse of power. In the 19th century, Burke was praised by both conservatives and liberals,[8] and in the 20th century, he became widely regarded—especially in the United States and the United Kingdom—as the philosophical founder of conservatism,[3][9] alongside Joseph de Maistre.[10][11] His writings and publications profoundly influenced British conservative thought and helped establish the earliest foundations for modern conservatism and liberal democracy.[12] Born in Dublin, Ireland, Burke’s mother, Mary, née Nagle, was a Roman Catholic from a County Cork family and cousin of Nano Nagle, while his father, Richard, a successful solicitor, was a member of the Church of Ireland. It remains unclear whether this is the same Richard Burke who converted from Catholicism.[13][14] The Burgh (Burke) dynasty traces its origins to the Anglo-Norman knight William de Burgh, who arrived in Ireland in 1185 following Henry II's 1171 invasion and is among the "chief Gall or Old English families that assimilated into Gaelic society"; the surname de Burgh (Latinised as de Burgo) was gaelicised in Irish as de Búrca or Búrc, which over time became Burke.[15] Burke adhered to his father's faith and remained a practising Anglican throughout his life, unlike his sister Juliana, who remained a Roman Catholic.[16] His political enemies repeatedly accused him of being educated at the Jesuit College of St. Omer, near Calais, France, and of harboring secret Catholic sympathies during a time when Catholicism disqualified individuals from public office under the Penal Laws in Ireland. As Burke told Frances Crewe: "Mr. Burke's Enemies often endeavoured to convince the World that he had been bred up in the Catholic Faith, & that his Family were of it, & that he himself had been educated at St. Omer—but this was false, as his father was a regular practitioner of the Law at Dublin, which he could not be unless of the Established Church: & it so happened that though Mr. B was twice at Paris, he never happened to go through the Town of St. Omer."[17] After being elected to the House of Commons, Burke took the required oaths of allegiance and abjuration, the oath of supremacy, and the declaration against transubstantiation.[13] As a child, Burke spent time with his mother's family near Killavullen in the Blackwater Valley, County Cork, and received his early education at a Quaker school in Ballitore, County Kildare, about 67 kilometres (42 mi) from Dublin; he may have attended a hedge school near Killavullen similar to his cousin Nano Nagle. He remained in correspondence with Mary Leadbeater, the daughter of the school's owner, throughout his life. In 1744, Burke began at Trinity College Dublin,[19] a Protestant institution that until 1793 did not permit Catholics to take degrees.[20] In 1747, he founded a debating society, Edmund Burke's Club, which merged in 1770 with Trinity's Historical Club to form the College Historical Society, the oldest undergraduate society in the world. The minutes of the meetings of Burke's Club are preserved in the Historical Society's collection. Burke graduated from Trinity in 1748. His father wanted him to study law, so he went to London in 1750 and entered the Middle Temple, but soon abandoned legal study to travel in Continental Europe. After abandoning law, he pursued a livelihood through writing. The late Lord Bolingbroke's Letters on the Study and Use of History was published in 1752 and his collected works in 1754, prompting Burke to write his first published work, A Vindication of Natural Society: A View of the Miseries and Evils Arising to Mankind, in Spring 1756. Burke imitated Bolingbroke's style and ideas in a reductio ad absurdum of his arguments for deistic rationalism to expose their absurdity.[22][23] Burke claimed that Bolingbroke's arguments against revealed religion could apply to all social and civil institutions as well.[24] Lord Chesterfield, Bishop Warburton, and others initially believed the work was genuinely by Bolingbroke rather than a satire.[22][25] All reviews were positive, with critics especially praising Burke's writing quality. Some reviewers failed to notice the ironic nature of the book, leading Burke to state in the preface to the second edition (1757) that it was a satire.[26] Richard Hurd believed the imitation was near-perfect and that it undermined Burke's purpose, arguing that an ironist should exaggerate to make ridicule shine through; he claimed that the Vindication was presented with such earnestness that half of Burke's purpose was sacrificed.[26] A minority of scholars argue that Burke actually wrote the Vindication in earnest and later disowned it for political reasons.[27][28] In 1757, Burke published A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful, a treatise on aesthetics that attracted attention from prominent Continental thinkers such as Denis Diderot and Immanuel Kant; it was his only purely philosophical work, completed in 1753.[29] When asked by Sir Joshua Reynolds and French Laurence to expand it thirty years later, Burke replied he was no longer fit for abstract speculation.[30] On 25 February 1757, Burke signed a contract with Robert Dodsley to write a "history of England from the time of Julius Caesar to the end of the reign of Queen Anne," consisting of eighty quarto sheets (640 pages), nearly 400,000 words, to be submitted by Christmas 1758.[31] He completed the work to the year 1216 and stopped; it was not published until after his death in an 1812 collection, An Essay Towards an Abridgement of the English History. G. M. Young dismissed the history, claiming it was "demonstrably a translation from the French."[32] Lord Acton commented on the story that Burke stopped his history because David Hume published his work, saying "it is ever to be regretted that the reverse did not occur."[33] During the year following the contract, Burke co-founded with Dodsley the influential Annual Register, a publication in which various authors evaluated international political events of the previous year.[34] The extent of Burke's contributions to the Annual Register is unclear.[35] Robert Murray cites the Register as evidence of Burke's opinions in his biography, while Philip Magnus does not directly reference it.[36] Burke remained the chief editor of the publication until at least 1789, and there is no evidence that any other writer contributed before 1766.[36] On 12 March 1757, Burke married Jane Mary Nugent (1734–1812), daughter of Dr. Christopher Nugent, a Catholic physician who had treated him in Bath. Their son Richard was born on 9 February 1758, and a second son, Christopher, born that December, died in infancy. Burke also helped raise a ward, Edmund Nagle (later Admiral Sir Edmund Nagle), the son of a maternal cousin who became orphaned in 1763.[38] Around this time, Burke was introduced to William Gerard Hamilton (known as "Single-speech Hamilton"). When Hamilton was appointed Chief Secretary for Ireland, Burke served as his private secretary for three years. In 1765, Burke became private secretary to Charles, Marquess of Rockingham, then Prime Minister of Great Britain, a close friend and associate until Rockingham's death in 1782. In December 1765, Burke entered the House of Commons as Member for Wendover in Buckinghamshire, a pocket borough under the patronage of Lord Fermanagh, later 2nd Earl Verney, a close political ally of Rockingham. After delivering his maiden speech, William Pitt the Elder said he had "spoken in such a manner as to stop the mouths of all Europe" and that the Commons should congratulate itself on acquiring such a Member.[40] The first major issue Burke addressed was the controversy with the American colonies, which escalated into war and eventual separation. In response to the 1769 Grenvillite pamphlet The Present State of the Nation, he published Observations on a Late State of the Nation, in which he surveyed the finances of France and predicted "some extraordinary convulsion in that whole system."[41] During the same year, with borrowed money, Burke purchased Gregories, a 600-acre (2.4 km²) estate near Beaconsfield. Although the estate included saleable assets such as art works by Titian, it proved a heavy financial burden in the following decades and Burke never fully repaid the purchase price. His speeches and writings led to the suggestion that he was the author of the Letters of Junius.[citation needed] Around this time, Burke joined the intellectual and artistic circle in London centered on Samuel Johnson, which also included David Garrick, Oliver Goldsmith, and Joshua Reynolds. Edward Gibbon described Burke as "the most eloquent and rational madman that I ever knew."[42] Although Johnson admired Burke's brilliance, he found him a dishonest politician.[43][44] Burke took a leading role in debates on the constitutional limits of royal executive power, arguing strongly against unrestrained royal authority and for the role of political parties in maintaining principled opposition to prevent abuses, either by the monarch or by factions within the government. His most important publication on this topic was Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents of 23 April 1770.[45] Burke identified the "discontents" as stemming from the "secret influence" of a neo-Tory group he labeled the "king's friends," whose system he called the "Double Cabinet," encompassing both exterior and interior administrations.[46] Britain needed a party with "an unshaken adherence to principle, and attachment to connexion, against every allurement of interest." Party divisions, "whether operating for good or evil, are things inseparable from free government."[47] In 1771, Burke drafted a bill giving juries the right to determine what constituted libel; he supported the bill, but it was opposed by some, including Charles James Fox, and did not become law. When introducing a similar bill in 1791 in opposition, Fox repeated almost verbatim the text of Burke's bill without acknowledgment.[48] Burke was instrumental in securing the right to publish parliamentary debates.[49] In a parliamentary debate on the prohibition of grain exports on 16 November 1770, Burke argued in favor of a free market in corn: "There are no such things as a high, & a low price that is encouraging, & discouraging; there is nothing but a natural price, which grain brings at an universal market."[50] In 1772, Burke played a key role in passing the Repeal of Certain Laws Act 1772, which repealed various old laws against dealers and forestallers in corn.[51] In the Annual Register for 1772 (published in July 1773), Burke condemned the partition of Poland, calling it "the first very great breach in the modern political system of Europe" and a disruption of the European balance of power.[52] On 3 November 1774, Burke was elected Member for Bristol, at the time "England's second city" with a large constituency in a genuine electoral contest.[53] At the conclusion of the poll, he delivered his Speech to the Electors of Bristol at the Conclusion of the Poll,[54] a notable disclaimer of the constituent-imperative form of democracy, substituting instead a statement of the "representative mandate" form.[55] He failed to win re-election in the 1780 general election. In May 1778, Burke supported a parliamentary motion revising restrictions on Irish trade. His constituents in Bristol urged him to oppose free trade with Ireland, but he resisted their protestations and stated: "If, from this conduct, I shall forfeit their suffrages at an ensuing election, it will stand on record an example to future representatives of the Commons of England, that one man at least had dared to resist the desires of his constituents when his judgment assured him they were wrong."[56] Burke published Two Letters to Gentlemen of Bristol on the Bills relative to the Trade of Ireland, in which he espoused "some of the chief principles of commerce; such as the advantage of free intercourse between all parts of the same kingdom ... the evils attending restriction and monopoly ... and that the gain of others is not necessarily our loss, but on the contrary an advantage by causing a greater demand for such wares as we have for sale."[57] He also supported Sir George Savile's efforts to repeal some of the penal laws against Catholics.[58] In 1776, Burke called capital punishment "the Butchery which we call justice," and in 1780 condemned the use of the pillory for two men convicted of attempting to practice sodomy.[38] His support for unpopular causes, including free trade with Ireland and Catholic emancipation, led to him losing his seat in 1780. For the remainder of his parliamentary career, he represented Malton, another pocket borough under the patronage of the Marquess of Rockingham. Burke expressed support for the grievances of the American Thirteen Colonies under the government of King George III and his appointed representatives. On 19 April 1774, he delivered a speech, "On American Taxation" (published in January 1775), on a motion to repeal the tea duty: "Again and again, revert to your old principles—seek peace and ensue it; leave America, if she has taxable matter in her, to tax herself. I am not here going into the distinctions of rights, nor attempting to mark their boundaries. I do not enter into these metaphysical distinctions; I hate the very sound of them. Leave the Americans as they anciently stood, and these distinctions, born of our unhappy contest, will die along with it .... Be content to bind America by laws of trade; you have always done it .... Do not burthen them with taxes.... But if intemperately, unwisely, fatally, you sophisticate and poison the very source of government by urging subtle deductions, and consequences odious to those you govern, from the unlimited and illimitable nature of supreme sovereignty, you will teach them by these means to call that sovereignty itself in question .... If that sovereignty and their freedom cannot be reconciled, which will they take? They will cast your sovereignty in your face. No body of men will be argued into slavery."[59] On 22 March 1775, Burke delivered a speech (published in May 1775) on reconciliation with America. He appealed for peace as preferable to civil war and reminded the House of Commons of America's growing population, industry, and wealth. He warned against the idea that Americans would back down under force, noting that most were of British descent: "The people of the colonies are descendants of Englishmen.... They are therefore not only devoted to liberty, but to liberty according to English ideas and on English principles. The people are Protestants ... a persuasion not only favourable to liberty, but built upon it .... My hold of the colonies is in the close affection which grows from common names, from kindred blood."

On 22 March 1775, Edmund Burke delivered a speech in the House of Commons advocating for peace with the American colonies, published in May 1775, emphasizing that reconciliation was preferable to civil war. He highlighted the growing population, industry, and wealth of the colonies, noting that the colonists were descendants of Englishmen, Protestants, and thus deeply devoted to liberty based on English principles. Burke stressed the strong ties between Britain and the colonies—rooted in common blood, privileges, and equal protection—that would ensure their loyalty, as long as the British government respected their civil rights and maintained a separation between sovereign authority and colonial privileges. He warned that if this balance was lost, the colonies would reject British rule and seek freedom elsewhere, as slavery was a "weed that grows in every soil" and could be found in any nation. Burke argued that peace should be simple, natural, and based on pacific principles, not achieved through war or endless negotiations. He presented four reasons against using force: first, resistance would be permanent, not temporary; second, Britain’s victory was uncertain, as "an armament is not a victory"; third, military action would damage the colonies’ land, rendering it unusable; fourth, Britain had no experience in subduing distant colonies by force. However, he identified the Americans' fierce love of freedom as the primary reason for avoiding war, describing them as acute, inquisitive, and resourceful. He proposed six resolutions to resolve the conflict peacefully, though they were not enacted before the outbreak of hostilities at Concord and Lexington in April 1775. Burke admired a passage in which he described an angel prophesying to Lord Bathurst the future greatness of both England and America, a passage that Samuel Johnson mocked with a devilish parody. When Lord North’s administration pursued military action, Burke was appalled by British celebrations of American defeats, claiming the national character was becoming authoritarian and less inquisitive and fiery. He condemned the British government for fighting "the American English" using "the hireling sword of German boors and vassals" to destroy colonial liberties, and stated he did not wish success to those who sought separation, as he opposed injustice, oppression, and absurdity. During the Gordon Riots in 1780, Burke became a target of hostility and his home was placed under military guard. After Lord North’s fall, Rockingham returned to power in March 1782, appointing Burke Paymaster of the Forces and a Privy Counsellor, though without a cabinet seat. Rockingham’s death in July 1782 and the rise of Shelburne ended the administration, but Burke introduced two Acts: the Paymaster General Act 1782, which ended the post as a sinecure by requiring Paymasters to deposit funds into the Bank of England before withdrawal and to submit monthly statements, and the Civil List and Secret Service Money Act 1782, a watered-down version of his original reform plan, which abolished 134 offices, including the third Secretary of State and the Board of Trade, limited pensions, and was expected to save £72,368 annually. In February 1783, Burke resumed the Paymaster role when Shelburne’s government fell, but after the coalition with Charles James Fox collapsed in 1783, he remained in opposition until the end of his political life. In his 1774 Speech to the Electors at Bristol, Burke defended representative government, asserting that representatives must serve the public interest above personal gain, and that their judgment, derived from conscience and reason, must not be overridden by constituents’ opinions. He rejected the idea that representatives should blindly follow instructions, emphasizing that Parliament is a deliberative body of one nation with one interest—the general good—rather than a congress of competing interests. Though Burke opposed slavery, he acknowledged that many of his electors profited from the slave trade, and he proposed a bill banning slaveholders from sitting in Parliament, describing slavery as a "weed that grows on every soil." He believed Africans were "barbaric" and needed civilisation through Christianity, and that slavery itself caused mental deficiency and uncivilised behaviour. He supported a gradual emancipation program called Sketch of a Negro Code, which Collins argues was detailed for its time and reflects a sincere, though gradualist, position. For over two decades, Burke pursued impeachment of Warren Hastings, Governor-General of Bengal, culminating in a trial beginning in 1786. Appointed Chairman of the Commons Select Committee on East Indian Affairs in 1781, he led investigations into injustices in Bengal, the war with Hyder Ali, and other Indian issues, producing reports that demanded Hastings’ recall and conveyed to Indian princes that Britain would not wage war against them. He described the Indian issue as beginning in commerce and ending in empire. In his famous 1785 speech, The Nabob of Arcot's Debts, he condemned the East India Company’s destruction of India’s water-based agricultural systems, which had been built by local rulers as monuments of benevolence and sustainability. He argued that Company rule had eroded these traditions and caused unnecessary suffering. On 4 April 1786, Burke presented the Article of Charge against Hastings, which led to the impeachment trial beginning in February 1788—the first major public discursive event on imperialism in England—where he portrayed Hastings as a "captain-general of iniquity" who caused famines and was likened to a "spider of Hell" and a "ravenous vulture." The House of Commons impeached Hastings, but the House of Lords acquitted him. Initially, Burke did not condemn the French Revolution; in a letter of 9 August 1789, he expressed admiration for its spirit, though he found its Parisian ferocity shocking. The events of 5–6 October 1789, when Parisian women marched on Versailles to force King Louis XVI to return to Paris, turned him against the revolution.

Burke's indictment, driven by emotional outrage, labeled Hastings a "captain-general of iniquity" who never dined without "creating a famine," whose heart was "gangrened to the core," and who resembled both a "spider of Hell" and a "ravenous vulture devouring the carcasses of the dead." The House of Commons eventually impeached Hastings, but the House of Lords acquitted him of all charges. Initially, Burke did not condemn the French Revolution; in a letter of 9 August 1789, he wrote: "England gazing with astonishment at a French struggle for Liberty and not knowing whether to blame or to applaud! The thing indeed, though I thought I saw something like it in progress for several years, has still something in it paradoxical and Mysterious. The spirit it is impossible not to admire; but the old Parisian ferocity has broken out in a shocking manner." The events of 5–6 October 1789, when a crowd of Parisian women marched on Versailles to compel King Louis XVI to return to Paris, turned Burke against the Revolution. In a letter to his son Richard Burke dated 10 October, he said: "This day I heard from Laurence who has sent me papers confirming the portentous state of France—where the Elements which compose Human Society seem all to be dissolved, and a world of Monsters to be produced in the place of it—where Mirabeau presides as the Grand Anarch; and the late Grand Monarch makes a figure as ridiculous as pitiable." On 4 November, Charles-Jean-François Depont wrote to Burke, requesting that he endorse the Revolution. Burke replied that any critical language of it by him should be taken "as no more than the expression of doubt," but he added: "You may have subverted Monarchy, but not recover'd freedom." In the same month, he described France as "a country undone." Burke's first public condemnation of the Revolution occurred during the debate in Parliament on the army estimates on 9 February 1790, provoked by praise of the Revolution by Pitt and Fox: "Since the House had been prorogued in the summer much work was done in France. The French had shewn themselves the ablest architects of ruin that had hitherto existed in the world. In that very short space of time they had completely pulled down to the ground, their monarchy; their church; their nobility; their law; their revenue; their army; their navy; their commerce; their arts; and their manufactures...[There was a danger of] an imitation of the excesses of an irrational, unprincipled, proscribing, confiscating, plundering, ferocious, bloody and tyrannical democracy...[In religion] the danger of their example is no longer from intolerance, but from Atheism; a foul, unnatural vice, foe to all the dignity and consolation of mankind; which seems in France, for a long time, to have been embodied into a faction, accredited, and almost avowed." In January 1790, Burke read Richard Price's sermon of 4 November 1789 entitled A Discourse on the Love of Our Country to the Revolution Society. That society had been founded to commemorate the Glorious Revolution of 1688. In this sermon, Price espoused the philosophy of universal "Rights of Men." Price argued that love of our country "does not imply any conviction of the superior value of it to other countries, or any particular preference of its laws and constitution of government." Instead, Price asserted that Englishmen should see themselves "more as citizens of the world than as members of any particular community." A debate between Price and Burke ensued that was "the classic moment at which two fundamentally different conceptions of national identity were presented to the English public." Price claimed that the principles of the Glorious Revolution included "the right to choose our own governors, to cashier them for misconduct, and to frame a government for ourselves." Immediately after reading Price's sermon, Burke wrote a draft of what eventually became Reflections on the Revolution in France. On 13 February 1790, a notice in the press said that shortly Burke would publish a pamphlet on the Revolution and its British supporters, but he spent the year revising and expanding it. On 1 November, he finally published the Reflections and it was an immediate best-seller. Priced at five shillings, it was more expensive than most political pamphlets, but by the end of 1790, it had gone through ten printings and sold approximately 17,500 copies. A French translation appeared on 29 November and on 30 November the translator Pierre-Gaëton Dupont wrote to Burke saying 2,500 copies had already been sold. The French translation ran to ten printings by June 1791. What the Glorious Revolution had meant was as important to Burke and his contemporaries as it had been for the last one hundred years in British politics. In the Reflections, Burke argued against Price's interpretation of the Glorious Revolution and instead, gave a classic Whig defence of it. Burke argued against the idea of abstract, metaphysical rights of humans and instead advocated national tradition: "The Revolution was made to preserve our antient indisputable laws and liberties, and that antient constitution of government which is our only security for law and liberty...The very idea of the fabrication of a new government, is enough to fill us with disgust and horror. We wished at the period of the Revolution, and do now wish, to derive all we possess as an inheritance from our forefathers. Upon that body and stock of inheritance we have taken care not to inoculate any cyon [scion] alien to the nature of the original plant...Our oldest reformation is that of Magna Charta. You will see that Sir Edward Coke, that great oracle of our law, and indeed all the great men who follow him, to Blackstone, are industrious to prove the pedigree of our liberties. They endeavour to prove that the ancient charter...were nothing more than a re-affirmance of the still more ancient standing law of the kingdom...In the famous law...called the Petition of Right, the parliament says to the king, 'Your subjects have inherited this freedom', claiming their franchises not on abstract principles 'as the rights of men', but as the rights of Englishmen, and as a patrimony derived from their forefathers." Burke said: "We fear God, we look up with awe to kings; with affection to Parliaments; with duty to magistrates; with reverence to priests; and with respect to nobility. Why? Because when such ideas are brought before our minds, it is natural to be so affected." Burke defended this prejudice on the grounds that it is "the general bank and capital of nations, and of ages" and superior to individual reason, which is small in comparison. "Prejudice", Burke claimed, "is of ready application in the emergency; it previously engages the mind in a steady course of wisdom and virtue, and does not leave the man hesitating in the moment of decision, sceptical, puzzled, and unresolved. Prejudice renders a man's virtue his habit." Burke criticised social contract theory by claiming that society is indeed a contract, although it is "a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born." The most famous passage in Burke's Reflections was his description of the events of 5–6 October 1789 and the part of Marie-Antoinette in them. Burke's account differs little from modern historians who have used primary sources. His use of flowery language to describe it provoked both praise and criticism. Philip Francis wrote to Burke saying that what he wrote of Marie-Antoinette was "pure foppery." Edward Gibbon reacted differently: "I adore his chivalry." Burke was informed by an Englishman who had talked with the Duchesse de Biron that when Marie-Antoinette was reading the passage she burst into tears and took considerable time to finish reading it. Price had rejoiced that the French king had been "led in triumph" during the October Days, but to Burke, this symbolised the opposing revolutionary sentiment of the Jacobins and the natural sentiments of those who shared his own view with horror—that the ungallant assault on Marie-Antoinette was a cowardly attack on a defenceless woman. Louis XVI translated the Reflections "from end to end" into French. Fellow Whig MPs Richard Sheridan and Charles James Fox disagreed with Burke and split with him. Fox thought the Reflections to be "in very bad taste" and "favouring Tory principles." Other Whigs such as the Duke of Portland and Earl Fitzwilliam privately agreed with Burke, but they did not wish for a public breach with their Whig colleagues. Burke wrote on 29 November 1790: "I have received from the Duke of Portland, Lord Fitzwilliam, the Duke of Devonshire, Lord John Cavendish, Montagu (Frederick Montagu MP), and a long et cetera of the old Stamina of the Whiggs a most full approbation of the principles of that work and a kind indulgence to the execution." The Duke of Portland said in 1791 that when anyone criticised the Reflections to him, he informed them that he had recommended the book to his sons as containing the true Whig creed. In the opinion of Paul Langford, Burke crossed something of a Rubicon when he attended a levee on 3 February 1791 to meet the King, later described by Jane Burke as follows: "On his coming to Town for the Winter, as he generally does, he went to the Levee with the Duke of Portland, who went with Lord William to kiss hands on his going into the Guards—while Lord William was kissing hands, The King was talking to The Duke, but his Eyes were fixed on [Burke] who was standing in the Crowd, and when He said His say to The Duke, without waiting for [Burke]'s coming up in his turn, The King went up to him, and, after the usual questions of how long have you been in Town and the weather, He said you have been very much employed of late, and very much confined. [Burke] said, no, Sir, not more than usual—You have and very well employed too, but there are none so deaf as those that w'ont hear, and none so blind as those that w'ont see—[Burke] made a low bow, Sir, I certainly now understand you, but was afraid my vanity or presumption might have led me to imagine what Your Majesty has said referred to what I have done—You cannot be vain—You have been of use to us all, it is a general opinion, is it not so Lord Stair? who was standing near. It is said Lord Stair;—Your Majesty's adopting it, Sir, will make the opinion general, said [Burke]—I know it is the general opinion, and I know that there is no Man who calls himself a Gentleman that must not think himself obliged to you, for you have supported the cause of the Gentlemen—You know the tone at Court is a whisper, but The King said all this loud, so as to be heard by every one at Court." Burke's Reflections sparked a pamphlet war. Mary Wollstonecraft was one of the first into print, publishing A Vindication of the Rights of Men a few weeks after Burke. Thomas Paine followed with the Rights of Man in 1791. James Mackintosh, who wrote Vindiciae Gallicae, was the first to see the Reflections as "the manifesto of a Counter Revolution." Mackintosh later agreed with Burke's views, remarking in December 1796 after meeting him that Burke was "minutely and accurately informed, to a wonderful exactness, with respect to every fact relating to the French Revolution." Mackintosh later said: "Burke was one of the first thinkers as well as one of the greatest orators of his time. He is without parallel in any age, excepting perhaps Lord Bacon and Cicero; and his works contain an ampler store of political and moral wisdom than can be found in any other writer whatever." In November 1790, François-Louis-Thibault de Menonville, a member of the National Assembly of France, wrote to Burke, praising Reflections and requesting more "very refreshing mental food" that he could publish. This Burke did in April 1791 when he published A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly. Burke called for external forces to reverse the Revolution and included an attack on the late French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau as being the subject of a personality cult that had developed in revolutionary France. Although Burke conceded that Rousseau sometimes showed "a considerable insight into human nature," he mostly was critical. Although he did not meet Rousseau on his visit to Britain in 1766–1767, Burke was a friend of David Hume, with whom Rousseau had stayed. Burke said Rousseau "entertained no principle either to influence of his heart, or to guide his understanding—but vanity"—which he "was possessed to a degree little short of madness." He also cited Rousseau's Confessions as evidence that Rousseau had a life of "obscure and vulgar vices" that was not "chequered, or spotted here and there, with virtues, or even distinguished by a single good action." Burke contrasted Rousseau's theory of universal benevolence and his having sent his children to a foundling hospital, stating that he was "a lover of his kind, but a hater of his kindred." These events and the disagreements that arose from them within the Whigs led to its break-up and to the rupture of Burke's friendship with Fox. In a debate in Parliament on Britain's relations with Russia, Fox praised the principles of the Revolution, although Burke was not able to reply at this time as he was "overpowered by continued cries of question from his own side of the House." When Parliament was debating the Quebec Bill for a constitution for Canada, Fox praised the Revolution and criticised some of Burke's arguments such as hereditary power. On 6 May 1791, Burke used the opportunity to answer Fox during another debate in Parliament on the Quebec Bill and condemn the new French Constitution and "the horrible consequences flowing from the French idea of the Rights of Man." Burke asserted that those ideas were the antithesis of both the British and the American constitutions. Burke was interrupted and Fox intervened, saying that Burke should be allowed to carry on with his speech. However, a vote of censure was moved against Burke for noticing the affairs of France which was moved by Lord Sheffield and seconded by Fox. Pitt made a speech praising Burke and Fox made a speech—both rebuking and complimenting Burke. He questioned the sincerity of Burke, who seemed to have forgotten the lessons he had learned from him, quoting from Burke's own speeches of fourteen and fifteen years before. Burke's response was as follows: "It certainly was indiscreet at any period, but especially at his time of life, to parade enemies, or give his friends occasion to desert him; yet if his firm and steady adherence to the British constitution placed him in such a dilemma, he would risk all, and, as public duty and public experience taught him, with his last words exclaim, 'Fly from the French Constitution.'" At this point, Fox whispered that there was "no loss of friendship." "I regret to say there is," Burke replied, "I have indeed made a great sacrifice; I have done my duty though I have lost my friend. There is something in the detested French constitution that envenoms every thing it touches." This provoked a reply from Fox, yet he was unable to give his speech for some time since he was overcome with tears and emotion. Fox appealed to Burke to remember their inalienable friendship, but he also repeated his criticisms of Burke and uttered "unusually bitter sarcasms." This only aggravated the rupture between the two men. Burke demonstrated his separation from the party on 5 June 1791 by writing to Fitzwilliam, declining money from him. Burke was dismayed that some Whigs, instead of reaffirming the principles of the Whig Party he laid out in the Reflections, had rejected them in favour of "French principles" and that they criticised Burke for abandoning Whig principles. Burke wanted to demonstrate his fidelity to Whig principles and feared that acquiescence to Fox and his followers would allow the Whig Party to become a vehicle for Jacobinism. Burke knew that many members of the Whig Party did not share Fox's views and he wanted to provoke them into condemning the French Revolution. Burke wrote that he wanted to represent the whole Whig Party "as tolerating, and by a toleration, countenancing those proceedings" so that he could "stimulate them to a public declaration of what every one of their acquaintance privately knows to be...their sentiments." On 3 August 1791, Burke published his Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs in which he renewed his criticism of the radical revolutionary programmes inspired by the French Revolution and attacked the Whigs who supported them as holding principles contrary to those traditionally held by the Whig Party. Burke owned two copies of what has been called "that practical compendium of Whig political theory," namely The Tryal of Dr. Henry Sacheverell (1710). Burke wrote of the trial: "It rarely happens to a party to have the opportunity of a clear, authentic, recorded, declaration of their political tenets upon the subject of a great constitutional event like that of the [Glorious] Revolution." Writing in the third person, Burke asserted in his Appeal: "[The] foundations laid down by the Commons, on the trial of Doctor Sacheverel, for justifying the revolution of 1688, are the very same laid down in Mr. Burke's Reflections; that is to say,—a breach of the original contract, implied and expressed in the constitution of this country, as a scheme of government fundamentally and inviolably fixed in King, Lords and Commons.—That the fundamental subversion of this antient constitution, by one of its parts, having been attempted, and in effect accomplished, justified the Revolution. That it was justified only upon the necessity."

Burke owned two copies of The Tryal of Dr. Henry Sacheverell (1710), which has been called "that practical compendium of Whig political theory." He wrote that it was rare for a party to have a clear, authentic, recorded declaration of its political tenets on a major constitutional event like the Glorious Revolution. In his Appeal, Burke asserted that the foundations laid by the Commons during the Sacheverell trial—such as a breach of the original contract implied and expressed in the constitution, justified the 1688 Revolution as a necessary response to a fundamental subversion of the ancient constitution by one of its parts, and that such a revolution was justified only as a means to restore and preserve the original contract of the British state. He used quotations from Paine's Rights of Man to illustrate what the New Whigs believed, and he genuinely believed that Foxite principles corresponded to Paine's. Burke denied that a majority of the people had or ought to have the final say in politics or society, stating that people had rights but also duties, which were not voluntary, and that the people could not overthrow morality derived from God. Although Whig grandees like Portland and Fitzwilliam privately agreed with Burke's Appeal, they wished he had used more moderate language; Fitzwilliam saw it as containing "the doctrines I have sworn by, long and long since." Francis Basset, a backbench Whig MP, wrote that he most perfectly differed from Mr. Fox and the great body of opposition on the French Revolution. Burke sent the Appeal to the King, who requested a friend to communicate that he had read it "with great satisfaction." Burke noted that no one from his party spoke, that they were secretly galled, agreed with him in principle but dared not speak out for fear of hurting Fox, and left him to himself, seeing that he could do himself justice. Charles Burney viewed the Appeal as "a most admirable book—the best & most useful on political subjects that I have ever seen," though he believed the differences between Burke and Fox should not be aired publicly. Eventually, most Whigs sided with Burke and supported William Pitt the Younger's Tory government, which responded to France's declaration of war by declaring war on Revolutionary France in 1793. In December 1791, Burke sent government ministers his Thoughts on French Affairs, arguing that no counter-revolution in France would arise from domestic causes; that the longer the Revolutionary Government existed, the stronger it became; and that its interest and aim was to disturb all other European governments. As a Whig, Burke did not wish to see an absolute monarchy restored in France after the collapse of Jacobinism. Writing to an émigré in 1791, he expressed that establishing the Ancien Régime—specifically, the system of Court Intrigue at Versailles—would be impossible, and that even if it were possible, it could not long endure. He believed that in one sense, nothing else could reasonably be done. On 28 December 1792, Burke delivered a speech in support of the Aliens Bill, which would exclude "murderous atheists, who would pull down Church and state; religion and God; morality and happiness," and in the peroration referenced a French order for 3,000 daggers. He revealed a dagger he had concealed in his coat and threw it to the floor, saying, "This is what you are to gain by an alliance with France," then picked it up and stated, "When they smile, I see blood trickling down their faces; I see their insidious purposes; I see that the object of all their cajoling is—blood! I now warn my countrymen to beware of these execrable philosophers, whose only object it is to destroy every thing that is good here, and to establish immorality and murder by precept and example—'Hic niger est hunc tu Romane caveto' ['Such a man is evil; beware of him, Roman']. Horace, Satires I. 4. 85." Burke supported the war against Revolutionary France, viewing it as a conflict between Britain and the revolutionaries governing France, not against the entire nation, and supported the royalist uprising in La Vendée, describing it on 4 November 1793 as "the sole affair I have much heart in," and urging Henry Dundas on 7 October to send reinforcements, though Dundas did not act. He believed the British government was not taking the uprising seriously enough, a view reinforced by a letter from the Prince Charles of France (S.A.R. le comte d'Artois) dated 23 October, requesting Burke to intercede, to which Burke replied on 6 November: "I am not in His Majesty's Service; or at all consulted in his Affairs." He published Remarks on the Policy of the Allies with Respect to France, stating: "I am sure every thing has shewn us that in this war with France, one Frenchman is worth twenty foreigners. La Vendée is a proof of this." On 20 June 1794, Burke received a vote of thanks from the House of Commons for his services in the Hastings Trial and immediately resigned his seat, being replaced by his son Richard. The loss of Richard in August 1794, to whom he was tenderly attached and saw as promising, was a blow. King George III, who had favored Burke due to his stance on the French Revolution, wished to create him Earl of Beaconsfield, but the death of his son prevented this honor; the only award he accepted was a pension of £2,500. This modest reward was attacked by the Duke of Bedford and the Earl of Lauderdale, to whom Burke replied in his Letter to a Noble Lord (1796): "It cannot at this time be too often repeated; line upon line; precept upon precept; until it comes into the currency of a proverb, To innovate is not to reform." He argued that his reward came from a mild and benevolent sovereign, while the Duke's came from inheritance from Henry the Eighth. He also warned of the consequences of implementing revolutionary ideas and described the English Constitution as a well-compacted structure, a fortress and temple, defended by reverence and power, which would stand inviolate against the "pickaxes of all the levellers of France." Burke's last publications were the Letters on a Regicide Peace (October 1796), which he regarded as appeasement, injurious to national dignity and honour. In his Second Letter, he wrote that the French Revolutionary government excluded individuality, was military in principle and spirit, and sought dominion over minds by proselytism and bodies by arms. This is held to be the first explanation of the modern concept of totalitarian state. Burke regarded the war with France as ideological, against an "armed doctrine," and believed France should not be partitioned due to its effect on European balance of power, and that the war was not against France but against the revolutionaries governing it. He stated: "It is not France extending a foreign empire over other nations: it is a sect aiming at universal empire, and beginning with the conquest of France." In November 1795, during a parliamentary debate on the high price of corn, Burke wrote a memorandum to Pitt. In December, Samuel Whitbread introduced a bill allowing magistrates to fix minimum wages, and Fox said he would vote for it. This debate likely prompted Burke to edit his memorandum, though he failed to complete a letter to Arthur Young on the subject, which was later inserted posthumously in 1800 as Thoughts and Details on Scarcity. In it, Burke expounded "some of the doctrines of political economists bearing upon agriculture as a trade," criticizing policies such as maximum prices and state regulation of wages, and stating that the State should confine itself to public matters—such as religion, magistracy, revenue, military force, corporations, public peace, safety, order, and prosperity. Adam Smith remarked that Burke was "the only man I ever knew who thinks on economic subjects exactly as I do, without any previous communications having passed between us." Writing to a friend in May 1795, Burke identified the causes of discontent as the malignity of Protestant ascendency in Ireland, Indianism in the East Indies, and Jacobinism across Europe, with Jacobinism being the greatest evil. By March 1796, he had changed his mind, stating that Indianism and Jacobinism were two enemies sapping the foundations of government, with Indianism being the worst and hardest to deal with, as it weakened the force needed to combat Jacobinism and provided Jacobinism with strong arms. For over a year before his death, Burke knew his stomach was "irrecoverably ruined"; he is believed to have had stomach cancer. After hearing of Burke's illness, Fox wrote to Mrs. Burke inquiring, and received the reply the next day: Mrs. Burke presented her compliments to Mr. Fox, thanked him, and communicated that it had cost Burke the most heart-felt pain to obey his duty in severing a long friendship, but that he deemed it necessary; that his principles remained unchanged; and that he would live for others, not himself. He believed his principles were necessary for the welfare and dignity of his country and could only be enforced through general persuasion of his sincerity. Burke died in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, on 9 July 1797 and was buried there alongside his son and brother. He married Jane Mary Nugent (1734–1812) in 1757; they had two sons, Christopher who died at age 5 and Richard who died at age 36. Jane managed Burke's household and was involved in his work. Burke is regarded by most political historians in the English-speaking world as a liberal conservative and the father of modern British conservatism. He was utilitarian and empirical in his arguments, while Joseph de Maistre was more providentialist and sociological with a confrontational tone. Burke believed property was essential to human life, and that the division of property formed the basis of social structure, helping develop control within a property-based hierarchy. He viewed social changes due to property as the natural order of human progress, and that the class system kept the monarch in check and that class was natural and part of a social agreement beneficial to all. Christopher Hitchens summarized that modern conservatism derives from Burke not only through appeals to property owners but also through appeals to an everyday interest in preserving the ancestral and immemorial. Burke's support for the causes of the "oppressed majorities," such as Irish Catholics and Indians, led to hostile criticism from Tories, while his opposition to the spread of the French Republic led to similar charges from Whigs, resulting in his isolation in Parliament. In the 19th century, Burke was praised by both liberals and conservatives. Philip Francis wrote that Burke "was a man who truly & prophetically foresaw all the consequences which would rise from the adoption of the French principles," though people doubted his arguments due to his passion. William Windham spoke from the same bench as Burke when he separated from Fox and was said to have spoken "like the ghost of Burke" against peace with France in 1801. William Hazlitt, a political opponent, regarded Burke as one of his three favorite writers (along with Junius and Rousseau) and made it a test of candor for opponents to allow Burke to be a great man. William Wordsworth initially supported the French Revolution and attacked Burke in A Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff (1793), but by the early 19th century admired him, calling him "the most sagacious Politician of his age," whose predictions "time has verified," and later revised The Prelude to include praise of Burke ("Genius of Burke! forgive the pen seduced/By specious wonders") and portrayed him as an old oak. Samuel Taylor Coleridge had previously criticized Burke in The Watchman but defended him in Friend (1809–1810) and in Biographia Literaria (1817) hailed him as a prophet and praised him.

Among his three favourite writers—along with Junius and Rousseau—Edmund Burke was regarded by some as a test of candour for those on the opposing side, demonstrating how deeply he was admired. William Wordsworth initially supported the French Revolution and attacked Burke in A Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff (1793), but by the early 19th century, he had changed his view and came to admire him, calling Burke "the most sagacious Politician of his age" whose predictions "time has verified." In Two Addresses to the Freeholders of Westmorland, Wordsworth praised Burke and later revised The Prelude to include the lines "Genius of Burke! forgive the pen seduced/By specious wonders," portraying him as an old oak. Samuel Taylor Coleridge, who had previously criticised Burke in The Watchman, defended him in Friend (1809–1810) and in Biographia Literaria (1817) hailed him as a prophet, praising his habit of referring to principles and calling him a "scientific statesman; and therefore a seer." Henry Brougham stated that all of Burke’s predictions, except one momentary expression, had been fulfilled, noting that anarchy and bloodshed ruled in France and conquest and convulsion devastated Europe, remarking that human providence rarely penetrates so far into the future. George Canning believed that Burke’s Reflections had been justified by subsequent events and that almost every prophecy had been strictly fulfilled; in 1823, he declared that he took Burke’s "last works and words [as] the manual of my politics." Conservative Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli was "deeply penetrated with the spirit and sentiment of Burke's later writings." William Gladstone considered Burke "a magazine of wisdom on Ireland and America" and in his diary recorded: "Made many extracts from Burke—sometimes almost divine." Richard Cobden often praised Burke's Thoughts and Details on Scarcity. Lord Acton considered Burke one of the three greatest Liberals, alongside Gladstone and Thomas Babington Macaulay. Lord Macaulay wrote in his diary: "I have now finished reading again most of Burke's works. Admirable! The greatest man since Milton." John Morley, a Gladstonian Liberal MP, published two books on Burke, including a biography, and was influenced by his views on prejudice. Francis Hirst, a Cobdenite Radical, believed Burke deserved a place among English libertarians, even though he was the most conservative and least abstract of reformers, always focused on preserving and renovating rather than innovating, likening him to a modern architect who restores an old house instead of demolishing it. Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France was controversial upon publication but after his death became his best-known and most influential work and a manifesto for Conservative thinking. Karl Marx, in a footnote to Volume One of Das Kapital, described Burke as a sycophant who, in the pay of the English oligarchy, praised the French Revolution as romantic and laudator temporis acti, and claimed that "The laws of commerce are the laws of Nature, and therefore the laws of God," calling him a vulgar bourgeois who "always sold himself in the best market." In Consistency in Politics, Winston Churchill wrote that Burke was both a foremost apostle of Liberty and a champion of Authority, and that a charge of political inconsistency was petty; he argued that Burke pursued the same ends and ideals, defending society from tyranny whether from a domineering monarch or a brutal mob. Historian Piers Brendon asserts that Burke laid the moral foundation for the British Empire, exemplified in the trial of Warren Hastings, which ultimately proved fatal, stating that Burke believed the British Empire must be governed on a plan of freedom, as it could only be governed by no other, a paternalistic doctrine that colonial government was a trust to be exercised for the benefit of subject people who would eventually attain freedom. Burke objected to the opium trade, calling it a "smuggling adventure" and condemning "the great Disgrace of the British character in India." According to political scientist Jennifer Pitts, Burke was arguably the first political thinker to conduct a comprehensive critique of British imperial practice in the name of justice for those suffering from its moral and political exclusions. However, other political scientists and literary theorists have challenged the extent of this critique, highlighting Burke’s strong support of British imperial practices in the New World. A Royal Society of Arts blue plaque commemorates Burke at 37 Gerrard Street, now in London's Chinatown. Statues of Burke are located in Bristol, England, Trinity College Dublin, and Washington, D.C., and he is the namesake of the Edmund Burke School, a private college preparatory school in Washington, D.C. Burke Avenue in The Bronx, New York, is named for him. Leo Strauss, a major critic of Burke, presented a harsh evaluation in his book Natural Right and History, noting that Burke separates happiness and virtue, grounding government in duties rather than "imaginary rights of man." Strauss viewed Burke as believing government should focus solely on duties, not on addressing individual needs or desires, and that government is a practicality, not a tool for improving human well-being. Strauss also argued that Burke rejects the use of logic, believing constitutions should be based on natural processes rather than rational planning, though he noted that this criticism undermines Burke’s own stance on tradition, as some human reason is inherent and grounded in tradition. Strauss did not fully support Burke’s view that legitimate social order arises only from a cumulative historical knowledge of past functions, and argued that Burke would oppose newly formed republics, though he acknowledged that Burke might have justified America’s constitution given its circumstances, while viewing France’s constitution as too radical due to its reliance on enlightened reasoning. Burke’s religious writings emphasize that religion is the foundation of civil society; he sharply criticised deism and atheism and promoted Christianity as a vehicle of social progress. Born in Ireland to a Catholic mother and a Protestant father, Burke vigorously defended the Church of England while showing sensitivity to Catholic concerns. He linked the preservation of a state-established religion with the preservation of constitutional liberties and highlighted Christianity’s benefits not only to the believer’s soul but also to political arrangements. The well-known maxim "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing" is widely misattributed to Burke. In 1770, Burke wrote in "Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents": "When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall, one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle." In 1867, John Stuart Mill made a similar statement in an inaugural address at the University of St Andrews: "Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing."
